content: The data on illnesses during early childhood was collected through maternal interviews. During the third phase of these interviews, mothers were asked to specify the duration of breastfeeding for their child by selecting one of the following categories: not at all, less than 6 months, 6 to 12 months, or longer than 12 months. For children aged 5 to 4 years, four subtest scores were assessed, including verbal reasoning, quantitative reasoning, abstract visual reasoning, and short-term memory. In many cases, the risk of bias was deemed unclear. The study by Song (2020) was a cross-sectional study based on data from the UNICEF-China Integrated Maternal and Child Health and Development (IMCHD) Project. A three-stage sampling procedure was used to select participants, involving administrative villages, natural villages, and households with children under 5 years old. A total of 4,488 children were surveyed. Breastfeeding indicators, such as duration and exclusivity, were assessed, and outcomes included obesity in children under 5 years of age, defined using WHO Child Growth Standards. The study by Sowole (2006) was a cross-sectional study conducted in urban and rural areas of Nigeria. Children aged 6 months to 5 years attending pediatric outpatient clinics or town halls were included. The study assessed breastfeeding history and its association with health outcomes. The Stendel-Hollis (2013) study was a cohort study conducted as part of the Women’s Health Initiative (WHI), which included over 168,000 postmenopausal women. Participants were classified based on their lactation history, including the number of children breastfed, age at first and last breastfeeding, and cumulative lifetime duration of lactation. Outcomes included various health conditions, and the risk of bias was evaluated. The Stordal (2017) study was a prospective cohort study conducted as part of the Norwegian Mother and Child Study (MoBa). It included singleton children whose parents completed questionnaires at 6 and 18 months of age. Breastfeeding duration was reported in intervals, and outcomes included the relative risks of infections such as acute gastroenteritis, otitis media, and respiratory tract infections. The Stuebe (2009) study was a prospective cohort study conducted as part of the Nurses’ Health Study (NHS). Participants reported their lactation history, including the total duration of breastfeeding across all pregnancies. Outcomes included the incidence of non-fatal myocardial infarction, coronary heart disease mortality, and other health conditions. The Suliga (2020) study was a cross-sectional study conducted as part of the Polish-Norwegian Study (PONS) project. It assessed breastfeeding duration and its association with metabolic syndrome, abdominal obesity, elevated glucose levels, and other health outcomes. The Tanaka (2012) study was a cross-sectional study conducted as part of the Fukuoka Child Health Study (FCHS) in Japan. It included children aged 3 years and assessed breastfeeding duration and its association with child health problems. The Taren (1993) study was a cross-sectional study conducted in Hubei Province, China, involving children aged 12 to 47 months. Breastfeeding duration and the timing of food introduction were recorded, and outcomes included nutritional and health indicators. The Taveras (2006) study was a prospective cohort study conducted as part of Project Viva in Massachusetts. It assessed breastfeeding practices and their association with infant growth and health outcomes. The Teele (1989) study was a prospective cohort study involving children under 3 months of age who were followed until 7 years of age. Breastfeeding duration and its association with middle ear disease were evaluated. The Tehrani (2014) study was a prospective cohort study conducted as part of the Tehran Lipid and Glucose Study (TLGS). It assessed lactation duration and its association with metabolic syndrome over a 9-year follow-up period. The Tryggvadottir (2001) study was a case-control study nested within a cohort of Icelandic women. It assessed breastfeeding duration and its association with breast cancer risk. The Vafa (2012) study was a cross-sectional study conducted in Tehran, Iran, involving 7-year-old children. Breastfeeding practices and their association with weight status were evaluated. The Vazquez-Nava (2008) study was a cross-sectional study conducted in Mexico, assessing feeding practices during the first year of life and their association with child health outcomes. The Veena (2010) study was a prospective cohort study conducted as part of the Mysore Parthenon study in India. It assessed breastfeeding duration and its association with cognitive function in children. In all studies, the risk of bias was evaluated, and in many cases, the risk was deemed unclear due to limitations in study design, data collection, or reporting.
